# Origin theory
Recently, we discussed the nature of loss. Not as existential as losing a living thing or of the immaterial... but the loss of material, and just how much material does change human life.

This leads to exciting threads about the nature of knowledge, our dependency on tools and craft, as natural problem-solvers; predictive processing somewhat suggests the brain is dedicated to solving problems, learning (somewhat primarily via error and feedback, not mere consumption. and noticing patterns which are necessary for prediction.

One of the first threads I'd like to unravel, is something I call origin theory. Basically this provides two ideas; one, how much of the original source could you recreate, if the original was lost? So that's studying the impermanance of the material world, especially technology, known for it's extreme memory power, but volatile hardware dependency. This also applies to general objects, things, materials and forms of storage and spaces, in keeping with the general spheres of theme in these studies, whilst avoiding the existential, becuase I clearly define the material and the living are not equal. More on that, in a separate study.


Origin theory (...apart from proving to be an incredibly useful cognitive tool, like occams razor for reasoning, but for recovering lost material) is also a metaphysical idea; how much do we depend on externalized structures, and how much of our work is in merely building tools to build our original idea, solve the original problem

Throughout those two primary points in origin theory, we see the same word re-appear as a natural consequence of the material. "Original."

Sometimes, the "negative space" created by the loss of things, is precisely the only frame at which we can see what was essential in the original, and what was not. This also ontogolically suggests something phenomenal, even if subjective; what we cannot remember may not have been significant. What did not reappear as patterns from the first origin, in the recreation (not stritly limited to recreating, but rather, continuity; a second or "nth" origin.) 

This treats the origin of all things, less of a prototype, and more of an implementation of an instance... in this case... it suggests alot of complex threads... but primarily, i think this is implementable and useful, by applying the two principles:
- One, we may avoid stress by understanding the impermanace of all things as a default condition which makes life possible; What is truly important, significant, and real, will persist beyond the lifetime of finite forms. In some sense, this suggests truth, knowledge, discovery and the essence of things, (...perhaps energy...) In essence, this principle observes how the essence of things cannot be destroyed nor created; we discover implementation of forms. Action: what is lost will reveal what truly mattered, once it reapears.
- Two, we may define a baseline of "value", by what is irreplaceable. (...still working on this...) but actionably; 

Forms cannot exist forever; according to physics (law of conservation of energy) "Energy cannot be created nor destroyed, it may only shift from one form to another."

In conclusion, a merged thesis to weave the threads in this pseudo-metaphysical study, is something I have been developing for a long while... "what is important, real or true, finds a way to reappear."

I think... this may suggest why we evolved to detect patterns, and why we can't function without patterns (...daily routine, seasons, cycles, music = patterns, etc. this is a study for another day!...)... patterns not only reveal structures that survive... but they reveal what is true... (...still working on this -!...)

Etymology of "origin" actually is significant, becuase the original or origin, actually means something like "birth" or "beginning"... something like "source"... from latin "origo".  ...however, it may not be "source" as in of the essence itself... I believe it is a source as in "here is a source of an instance, the way a github server is a source for changes, but not the source of files itself." 

In some sense, exclusion, negative-space, or the absence of something, could be described as an filtering of the ontological; we may only notice things, their function, or their significance, when their form dissapears from our continuity...(...not sure about these notes, but working on them...)

Even more significantly... how do we learn? How do we synthesize the very information we sought to archive, and integrate it into the being? Into action? Into transformation of the psyche and the person? I believe this is where Origin theory somewhat suggests the most implementable idea; when we no longer rely on the source material for reference, then the knowledge has become integrated. 

However, this is indistinguishable from memorization, which is not the same as integration... and it presents the  same issue of information/material obsession (...that's another branch for another day...)

In this sense, information storage is only as necessary, insofar as is it retrieved. Information, merely for collection or storage... the accumulation of wealth, or the general obsession to secure the impermanace of things... is almost indistinguishable from hoarding. That has it's own set of implications.

Here is a counterbalance so Origin theory does not expand into "everything is metaphysics" territory; the problem of forgetting. If we remember what was significant, why do we often forget what is important? Not passwords, or details... but significant chunks of continuity? That's a completely different study outside of Origin theory! If Origin studies the

In some sense, our memory is the last space we have for our cartography of life... in some sense, our memories serve as distributed points of continuity, such that they form coheive shapes (constellation-like) in an endless phenomenological cartography...

When we no longer have an external medium of externalization, we turn inwards.. and that's where Kybernetics becomes incredible useful, becusae it studies how we navigate our own inner nonfinite spaces of information! (...but that's definitely too far for the scope of this study -!...)

Origin Theory, applications in learning, education, philosophy of things, dealing with loss and applied ontology+metaphysics.

Application scenario: "if you lost all your work tomorrow, would you give up or would you continue? (completion vs. continuity). Would you start over from zero, or start again? (that's a significantly different perspective, and it's almost "Sisyphus"-like.) Could you recreate and relearn from the original structures? Or would you become dependent on what previous versions of you could only do?" 

Here is the emphasis behind the metaphysics and crazy theories: This hopefully counters or mitigates alot of modern stress we human beings are facing, as a result of living in an information-dense world, with insufficient problem-solving models and knowledge. Infact, Origin theory may be a proposition for GPS: General Problem Solving. It should proobably be as essential a field as mathematics and english!
